one_sentence_story: With a 50-millisecond 3×4 letter flash followed by a post-flash High, Medium, or Low tone at Harvard in 1960, George Sperling discovered Iconic Memory — proving early visual cortex holds ~9 of 12 letters in a vivid ghost buffer that fades within 300–500 milliseconds before working memory can copy more than four.
so_what_for_you: When glancing briefly at critical numbers (a license plate, slide formula, or room code), decide in advance WHICH 3–4 digits to grab first — and stop rapid-scrolling bright screens, which bleach away iconic traces before a single idea consolidates.

jargon_map.plain: high-capacity (~9–10+ items), ultra-brief (~300–500 ms) visual sensory buffer holding a fading ghost image in retina/V1 after a scene disappears
jargon_map.analogy: wet ink glowing on a radar screen for a third of a second before fading

jargon_map.plain: asking subjects to recite all 12 flashed letters — bottlenecked at ~4.5 because the ghost image fades while speaking the first four
jargon_map.analogy: trying to bucket all the rain off a roof before it runs down the gutter

jargon_map.plain: playing a High, Medium, or Low audio tone AFTER the screen goes blank to sample just one random 4-letter row — revealing ~76% (~9.1/12) was actually available.
jargon_map.analogy: dipping one test-cup anywhere along the roof to prove the whole roof was wet

jargon_map.plain: rapid drop of Partial-Report superiority down to the 4.5-item Whole-Report floor when the audio tone is delayed past 0.3–0.5 seconds
jargon_map.analogy: the half-second lifespan of raw visual persistence

jargon_map.plain: erasing the 300-ms iconic ghost image prematurely when a bright new visual flash overwrites V1 immediately afterward
jargon_map.analogy: scrolling to the next bright slide before your brain copies the last one
